s: A company runs an application in a primary AWS Region and maintains a pilot light disaster recovery (DR) environment in a secondary Region. The company uses an organization in AWS Organizations with all features enabled to manage its cloud environment. The company uses AWS CloudFormation to deploy resources to both Regions. During a test, the company cannot fail over to the DR Region within the company's RTO target of 60 minutes because the DR Region's infrastructure has experienced configuration drift. The company observes drift in security groups, AMI versions, and application configurations. The configuration drift between the two Regions causes a delay of 30 to 45 minutes to scale up to production levels. The company needs an automated solution to prevent configuration drift so the company can fail over to the DR Region within the target RTO. Which solution will meet this requirement?
o: Deploy CloudFormation cross-Region stack sets in both Regions. Implement SCPs and IAM policies to restrict infrastructure modifications. Use Amazon EC2 Image Builder to create AMIs and distribute them to the DR Region. Configure AWS Config rules in both Regions. Set up Amazon EventBridge rules that invoke AWS Systems Manager Automation runbooks to remediate drift when drift is detected. Store application configurations in AWS Secrets Manager and enable cross-Region replication.

Use AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store to manage resource configurations centrally. Use AWS Lambda functions to synchronize AMIs between Regions daily. Use Amazon CloudWatch alarms to detect configuration changes. Use AWS CodePipeline to deploy configuration updates manually when drift is detected.

Deploy CloudFormation cross-Region stack sets in both Regions. Use SCPs to enforce configuration consistency. Use AWS Backup to replicate AMIs to the DR Region. Use AWS Config to scan for configuration drift daily. Use custom scripts to remediate configuration differences when drift is detected. Store application configurations in an Amazon S3 bucket and enable cross-Region replication to the DR Region.

Use Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling launch templates that have versioning enabled to maintain configuration consistency. Use AWS CloudTrail to log all configuration changes. Use AWS Health Dashboard to monitor infrastructure events. Use AWS Well-Architected Tool reviews quarterly to identify drift. Store application configurations in an Amazon S3 bucket and enable cross-Region replication to the DR Region.
e: Option A is correct because the problem is not simply disaster recovery capacity; it is configuration drift that delays failover. CloudFormation StackSets provide consistent infrastructure deployment across accounts and Regions. SCPs and IAM policies reduce unauthorized manual changes. EC2 Image Builder standardizes AMI creation and distribution to the DR Region. AWS Config detects noncompliant resources, and EventBridge with Systems Manager Automation can remediate drift automatically instead of waiting for manual correction during a DR event. Replicating application configuration through Secrets Manager keeps runtime settings aligned across Regions. Option B still depends on manual deployment. Option C uses daily scans and custom scripts, which may miss urgent drift and adds operational risk. Option D mostly logs or reviews issues but does not automatically prevent or remediate drift.

w.y: The need is to stop drift in security groups, AMIs and app configuration between Regions automatically. StackSets keep infrastructure in sync, Image Builder distributes AMIs, Config with EventBridge and Systems Manager Automation fixes drift, and Secrets Manager replication keeps configuration aligned.

o.A: Correct: StackSets, guardrails, Image Builder, Config with automated remediation, and replicated configuration.
o.B: Manual deployments when drift is found are not automated prevention.
o.C: Daily scans and custom scripts leave drift in place between runs and add work.
o.D: Quarterly reviews and Health Dashboard do not detect or fix configuration drift.
